questions.prompt: Someone generates each audio sample as the sine of an angle computed from `n`, a float32 sample counter that counts up for ever. At 48 kHz, roughly when can float32 no longer represent every integer value of `n`, so repeated float32 additions of one can stop advancing the counter?

options.text: After about 43.7 seconds
options.explanation: That would be 2²¹ samples. Float32 represents every integer up to 2²⁴.

options.text: After about 24 hours
options.explanation: Integers stop being exact much earlier than that; the 24-bit significand runs out at 16.8 million.

options.text: Never, because integers are always exact in floating point
options.explanation: Only integers up to 2²⁴ (16,777,216) are all exactly representable in float32.

options.text: After about 5.8 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 samples; 16,777,216 / 48,000 ≈ 349.5 s ≈ 5.8 minutes. Beyond that, `n + 1` can round back to `n`.

questions.workedExample:
1. Float32 significand: 24 bits (23 stored + 1 implicit).
2. All integers up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216 are exact; above that, only even numbers are, and so on.
3. Time to reach it:

```formula
t = 2^{24} / f_s
t = 16777216 / 48000 Hz ≈ 349.5 s
where
t: the time until the counter passes the last exactly representable run of integers, in seconds (s)
2^{24}: 16,777,216, the largest integer up to which float32 can represent every whole number
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 samples per second
≈: approximately equal to
Hz: hertz, per second
s: seconds
In words: at 48,000 samples a second the counter reaches 16.8 million after about 350 seconds, about 5.8 minutes.
```

Even while the counter’s integer values remain exact, computing a large angle in float32 can lose fractional-phase precision. That is separate from the repeated-addition counter stall; an unwrapped phase accumulator has the additional step-rounding error demonstrated in this unit. Keep a wrapped phase instead of a growing counter.

lessons.title: Choosing an oscillator reset policy
lessons.body:
## From oscillator to instrument

A practical oscillator also needs:

- **Band-limiting** for saw, square and pulse, or high notes alias badly (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units).
- **Smoothed or per-sample frequency** so pitch changes don't step audibly (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units).
- A **reset policy**: resetting phase on each note-on gives a consistent attack; free-running sounds more like analogue oscillators. Both are valid choices.

Libraries such as DaisySP (`Oscillator`) and the Teensy Audio Library (`AudioSynthWaveform`) provide alias-reducing waveform options and a way to set or reset phase. In the source revisions checked on 2026-10-16 (DaisySP 2c72eaf9eac5, PJRC Audio 3039be2773e8), the basic frequency setters recompute an increment without a pitch smoother, so smoothing remains your job. The roadmap suggests writing your own sine oscillator first, then comparing with a library's.

## Key takeaways

- Resetting at silent note starts makes attacks repeatable; free-running phase varies starts.
- Resetting an audible oscillator can click; band-limiting and smoothing remain separate requirements.

## Further reading

- [Oscillator interface — DaisySP](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electro-smith/DaisySP/2c72eaf9eac5fc0dca1919d65d606da907832618/Source/Synthesis/oscillator.h)
- [Waveform interface — PJRC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PaulStoffregen/Audio/3039be2773e86daf1f381a1e8bdc1e6a55ed11f1/synth_waveform.h)

questions.prompt: You're deciding whether each oscillator's phase should reset to 0 on note-on or run freely. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Resetting gives the same attack waveform every note, which suits punchy basses and drums
options.explanation: Correct. Every note starts at the same point in the cycle, so attacks are consistent.

options.text: Resetting phase on note-on can never cause a click
options.explanation: If the voice is still sounding (e.g. a legato retrigger or a stolen voice), jumping the phase to 0 can change the output value abruptly and click; a specially timed reset can leave the value unchanged.

options.text: With two detuned free-running oscillators, the beating pattern differs from note to note
options.explanation: Correct. Their relative phase at note-on is effectively random, so the beating starts at a different point each time.

options.text: Free-running oscillators make each note's start slightly different, similar to many analogue synths
options.explanation: Correct. The phase at note-on depends on timing, giving natural variation.

options.text: Free-running oscillators must be stopped between notes to save CPU, so they can't really free-run
options.explanation: A free-running oscillator only needs its phase advanced; whether you process silent voices is a separate CPU decision.

questions.workedExample:
Consider what the listener hears at note start:

- **Reset:** identical start every time. Predictable, punchy, can click if the voice was already sounding.
- **Free-run:** start point varies. More organic; detuned oscillators beat differently each note.

Many synths make it a per-patch option. Either way, a phase jump on a *sounding* voice can create an output-value discontinuity, so pair resets with an envelope starting from silence or a short fade.

lessons.title: Periodic sounds as Fourier series
lessons.body:
Play a sine, a triangle, a square and a sawtooth at the same pitch and loudness. Each sounds clearly different: the sine pure, the triangle soft, the square hollow, the saw buzzy and bright. Pitch and loudness are equal, so the difference is **timbre**, and for steady periodic tones timbre is largely set by the **spectrum**: which frequencies are present, and how strong each one is.

This lesson gives you the spectra of the standard waveforms and a way to verify them. Every later block (band-limiting, filters) is easier to reason about in these terms.

## Fourier series for ordinary periodic audio signals

A nonconstant periodic waveform has a fundamental frequency of one divided by its shortest repeating period, and, under the usual Fourier-series conditions for piecewise-smooth signals, it can be represented by a mean plus sinusoidal components at whole-number multiples of that repeat rate. At an ideal jump the series takes the midpoint of the one-sided limits:

```formula
f_0 = 1 / T
x(t) = DC + Σ A_n sin(2πn f_0 t + φ_n)
where
f_0: the fundamental frequency, in hertz (Hz): how many times per second the waveform repeats
T: the period, the time one repeat takes, in seconds (s)
x(t): the value of the waveform at time t
t: time, in seconds (s)
DC: the waveform's mean (average) value, a constant offset; zero for the centred waveforms here
Σ: sigma, "sum of": add up the term after it for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on (in principle for ever)
n: the harmonic number, a whole number 1, 2, 3...; component n has frequency n × f_0
A_n: the amplitude (peak height) of component n
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
π: pi, about 3.14159; 2π radians is one full cycle
φ_n: phi n, the phase of component n: where in its cycle that sine starts, in radians
·: multiplication, the same as ×
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
s: seconds
In words: any repeating wave equals its average plus a stack of sines at 1, 2, 3... times the repeat rate, each with its own height and starting point.
```

For example, a wave repeating every 10 milliseconds has a 100 Hz repeat rate. Its non-DC components lie on the 100, 200, 300 Hz grid and so on; some may have zero amplitude.

- DC is the mean value (zero for the centred waveforms here).
- The first harmonic is the **fundamental**; perceived pitch need not equal the strongest component.
- The second and higher harmonics are the **overtones**. “Harmonic” also includes the fundamental, so these words are not identical labels.
- Every component has its own amplitude and phase.

This is the **Fourier series**. Intuitively: a single sinusoid has one non-zero positive-frequency component, while a more complicated periodic waveform requires more components (and possibly a DC mean). The sharper the features of a waveform (corners, jumps), the more high harmonics it needs to build them.

The *magnitudes* A_n plotted against frequency form the **magnitude spectrum**: a row of spikes at multiples of `f0`, each with a height.

## Key takeaways

- A periodic sound can be decomposed into a mean plus harmonics with individual phases and magnitudes.
- Its repeat rate sets the harmonic grid; the strongest component need not be the perceived pitch.

## Further reading

- [Fourier series — Julius O. Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Fourier_Series_FS_Relation.html)
- [Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF](https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.16)

questions.prompt: A periodic test signal repeats every 10 milliseconds. Which frequency grid can its Fourier-series components occupy?

options.text: 100 Hz, 200 Hz, 300 Hz and further whole multiples of 100 Hz, plus a possible DC mean.
options.explanation: Correct. Ten milliseconds is one hundredth of a second, so the repeat rate is 100 cycles per second. A Fourier series uses that rate and its whole multiples, with a separate constant mean.

options.text: Only 10 Hz.
options.explanation: The period is a time, not a frequency. Taking its reciprocal gives 100 Hz, and a complex waveform can have harmonics.

options.text: Any unrelated frequencies, such as 141 Hz and 237 Hz.
options.explanation: Those components would not repeat consistently on the stated ten-millisecond grid. The claim concerns an exactly periodic signal.

options.text: Only 100 Hz, because harmonics would change the period.
options.explanation: Whole multiples complete an integer number of cycles in ten milliseconds, so they can share the same repeating period.

questions.workedExample: One second contains one hundred ten-millisecond periods. A 200 Hz component completes two cycles in each period, while a 300 Hz component completes three. Their sum still repeats every ten milliseconds. Some coefficients may be zero, and a constant mean can be present.

lessons.title: Fourier series and harmonic patterns
lessons.body:
A waveform’s harmonic amplitudes explain much of its steady timbre. This unit compares the ideal saw, square and triangle at the same fundamental frequency.

## The standard waveforms

| Wave | Harmonics present | Relative amplitude pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Sine | Fundamental only | No upper harmonics |
| Saw | All whole harmonics | Inverse harmonic number |
| Square | Odd harmonics | Inverse harmonic number |
| Triangle | Odd harmonics | Inverse square of harmonic number |

For waves swinging between −1 and +1, the standard series are:

```formula
ω = 2πf_0
x_saw(t) = (2 / π)
  × Σ (−1)^{(n + 1)} sin(nωt) / n
x_sq(t) = (4 / π) Σ sin(nωt) / n
x_tri(t) = (8 / π^2)
  × Σ (−1)^k sin(nωt) / n^2
where
ω: omega, the angular frequency of the fundamental, in radians per second: 2π radians per cycle times f_0 cycles per second
f_0: the fundamental frequency, in hertz (Hz)
π: pi, about 3.14159
x_saw(t), x_sq(t), x_tri(t): the ideal sawtooth, square and triangle series; at discontinuities the series takes the midpoint; finite truncations may overshoot the ideal extrema
t: time in seconds, measured from a point where the wave crosses zero going upwards
Σ: sigma, "sum of": for the saw add the term for every n = 1, 2, 3...; for the square and triangle add it for odd n only (1, 3, 5...)
n: the harmonic number
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
(−1)^{n+1}: a sign that alternates +, −, +, − for n = 1, 2, 3, 4...
k: for the triangle, (n − 1) / 2, so (−1)^{k} alternates +, −, + for n = 1, 3, 5
·: multiplication, the same as ×
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: the saw has every harmonic at 1/n of the fundamental's strength, the square has only odd harmonics at 1/n, and the triangle has only odd harmonics at the much faster-falling 1/n^2.
```

The series scale factors give each ideal waveform’s fundamental amplitude:

```formula
A_saw = 2 / π ≈ 0.637
A_sq = 4 / π ≈ 1.273
A_tri = 8 / π^2 ≈ 0.811
where
A_saw, A_sq, A_tri: the fundamental’s peak amplitude for the ideal saw, square and triangle normalised to extrema of minus and plus one
π: pi, about 3.14159
≈: approximately equal to; values are rounded
In words: equal ideal peak extrema do not imply equal fundamental strengths.
```

 The alternating signs are phases; they shape the waveform but not the magnitude spectrum. The saw series shown ramps upward with its jump halfway through a cycle measured from the upward zero crossing. Its shift relative to the earlier phase-function saw changes phases, not harmonic magnitudes. The triangle here also starts at an upward zero crossing, rather than at the minimum used by the earlier phase-function triangle.

To compare harmonics by ear it helps to convert their relative amplitudes into decibels:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(A_n / A_1)
L = 20 log_10(1/2) ≈ −6.0 dB
L = 20 log_10(1/9) ≈ −19.1 dB
where
L: the level of harmonic n relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB); negative means quieter
A_n: the amplitude of harmonic n
A_1: the amplitude of the fundamental
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to to get the number, so log_10(0.1) = −1
20: the factor that converts an amplitude ratio to decibels
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: halving an amplitude is about −6 dB; the saw's 2nd harmonic (1/2) is −6 dB and the triangle's 3rd (1/9) is about −19 dB.
```

What this means for the sound:

- **Saw** has every harmonic, falling at 6 dB per octave of harmonic number (each doubling of the harmonic number halves the amplitude). This is the brightest standard wave and the usual starting point for subtractive brass, strings and basses.
- **Square** has only odd harmonics with the same reciprocal-harmonic-number decay. Missing even harmonics give its hollow, woody, clarinet-like character.
- **Triangle** also has only odd harmonics, but they fall at the reciprocal of harmonic number squared, i.e. 12 dB per octave. The 3rd harmonic is 1/9 of the fundamental (−19 dB), so it sounds close to a sine.

## Key takeaways

- Fourier series describes periodic waves using DC and harmonics with magnitudes and phases.
- Saw harmonics decay by harmonic number; triangle harmonics decay faster than square harmonics.

## Further reading

- [Blofeld user manual — Waldorf](https://downloads.waldorfmusic.com/cloud/index.php/s/32zdTsdYcRSX9eE/download)
- [Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF](https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.16)

questions.prompt: Which description matches the spectrum of an ideal square wave?

options.text: All harmonics, amplitudes inversely proportional to harmonic number
options.explanation: That is the sawtooth. The square's symmetry cancels every even harmonic.

options.text: Odd harmonics only, amplitudes inversely proportional to the square of harmonic number
options.explanation: That is the triangle, whose harmonics fall much faster.

options.text: Odd harmonics only, amplitudes inversely proportional to harmonic number
options.explanation: Correct. 1, 3, 5, 7... at 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental. The missing evens give the hollow sound.

options.text: Only the fundamental
options.explanation: That is a sine wave; a square has sharp jumps that need many harmonics.

questions.workedExample:
From the Fourier series of a ±1 square wave:

```formula
x_sq(t) = (4 / π) Σ sin(nωt) / n
where
x_sq(t): the ideal square-wave Fourier series; at jumps its value is the midpoint; using only a finite number of terms can overshoot
π: pi, about 3.14159
Σ: sigma, "sum of": add the term for every odd n (1, 3, 5...)
n: the harmonic number; only odd values appear
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
ω: omega, the fundamental's angular frequency, 2π × f_0 radians per second
t: time, in seconds
f_0: the fundamental frequency, in hertz
·: multiplication
In words: odd harmonics only, each with amplitude 1/n of the fundamental's.
```

Harmonic n has amplitude the reciprocal of harmonic number relative to the fundamental, and even n is missing:

```
n:    1   2   3    4   5
amp:  1   0   1/3  0   1/5
```

Odd only, falling as the reciprocal of harmonic number. Compare the triangle (odd, the reciprocal of harmonic number squared) and saw (all, the reciprocal of harmonic number).

questions.prompt: A sawtooth plays at 200 Hz. How strong is its 600 Hz component relative to the fundamental, in dB?

options.text: About −9.5 dB
options.explanation: Correct. 600 Hz is the 3rd harmonic; saw harmonics fall as the reciprocal of harmonic number, so its amplitude is 1/3 of the fundamental, which is about −9.5 dB.

options.text: About −19 dB
options.explanation: That is 1/9 (the reciprocal of harmonic number squared), the triangle rule, not the saw.

options.text: 0 dB, because all harmonics are equally loud
options.explanation: A saw's harmonics get weaker with n. Equal-strength harmonics would describe an impulse train.

options.text: It is absent, because saws contain only odd harmonics
options.explanation: The *square* lacks even harmonics. A saw has all of them, and in any case 3 is odd.

questions.workedExample:
1. Harmonic number: 600 / 200 = **3**.
2. Saw amplitude rule: the reciprocal of harmonic number, so the 3rd harmonic is **1/3** of the fundamental.
3. Convert to decibels:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(A_n / A_1)
L = 20 log_10(1/3) ≈ −9.54 dB
where
A_n: the amplitude of harmonic n, here the 3rd
A_1: the amplitude of the fundamental
L: the level relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB); negative means quieter
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to to get the number
20: the factor that converts an amplitude ratio into decibels
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a component at one third of the fundamental's amplitude is about 9.5 dB quieter.
```

questions.prompt: Why does a triangle wave sound much closer to a sine than a square wave does, even though both contain only odd harmonics?

options.text: The triangle has fewer harmonics than the square
options.explanation: Both have infinitely many odd harmonics in the ideal case. The difference is how fast they fall.

options.text: Its harmonics fall as the reciprocal of harmonic number squared, so the 3rd is only 1/9 (−19 dB) and the 5th 1/25 (−28 dB) of the fundamental
options.explanation: Correct. The fundamental dominates far more than in the square, where the 3rd is 1/3 (−9.5 dB).

options.text: A triangle's harmonics are out of phase with each other, which cancels them
options.explanation: The alternating signs are phases; they affect the shape, not the magnitude of each harmonic.

options.text: A triangle has only even harmonics, which blend with the fundamental
options.explanation: A triangle has *odd* harmonics, the same set as a square.

questions.workedExample:
Compare the 3rd and 5th harmonics:

| | 3rd | 5th |
|---|---|---|
| Square (the reciprocal of harmonic number) | −9.5 dB | −14 dB |
| Triangle (the reciprocal of harmonic number squared) | −19 dB | −28 dB |

Each entry comes from the decibel formula; for example, the triangle's 3rd harmonic:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(1 / n^2)
L = 20 log_10(1/9) ≈ −19.1 dB
where
n: the harmonic number, here 3
L: the level relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB); negative means quieter
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to to get the number
20: the factor that converts an amplitude ratio into decibels
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a 1/9-amplitude harmonic is about 19 dB below the fundamental, so the triangle's overtones are faint.
```

The triangle's energy is overwhelmingly in the fundamental, so it sounds soft and nearly pure.

lessons.title: Oscillator pulse width and missing harmonics
lessons.summary: Oscillator pulse width and missing harmonics.
lessons.body:
### Pulse waves

A pulse wave's harmonics depend on its width (the fraction of each cycle it spends high):

```formula
A_n ∝ |sin(π n w)| / n
where
A_n: the amplitude of harmonic n
∝: "is proportional to": A_n equals the right-hand side times a fixed scale factor
|x|: the absolute value of x, i.e. x without its sign
sin: the sine function, taking an angle in radians
π: pi, about 3.14159
n: the harmonic number, 1, 2, 3...
w: the oscillator pulse width, a fraction of the cycle between 0 and 1 (0.5 is a square wave)
In words: each harmonic's strength falls roughly as 1/n, but is multiplied by a sine that reaches zero whenever n × w is a whole number.
```

A harmonic vanishes whenever its number times the width is a whole number. At half-cycle width, all even harmonics vanish. At quarter-cycle width, every fourth harmonic vanishes, because the fourth harmonic spans a whole cycle during the high interval. This is why sweeping oscillator pulse width changes the timbre so audibly.

## Key takeaways

- Oscillator pulse width changes the harmonic strengths.
- At one-third duty cycle, every third harmonic vanishes in the ideal series.

## Further reading

- [Blofeld user manual — Waldorf](https://downloads.waldorfmusic.com/cloud/index.php/s/32zdTsdYcRSX9eE/download)
- [Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)

questions.prompt:
A pulse wave has a width of 1/3 (one third of a cycle spent high). Using the lesson's rule for pulse harmonics, which harmonics are missing?

```formula
A_n ∝ |sin(π n w)| / n
where
A_n: the amplitude of harmonic n
∝: is proportional to
|x|: absolute value: x without its sign
sin: the sine function (angle in radians)
π: pi, about 3.14159
n: the harmonic number, 1, 2, 3...
w: the oscillator pulse width, as a fraction of the cycle
In words: harmonic n's strength is about 1/n times a sine that is zero whenever n × w is whole.
```

options.text: All even harmonics (2, 4, 6...)
options.explanation: That is the half-cycle duty case: a square wave.

options.text: Every 3rd harmonic (3, 6, 9...)
options.explanation: Correct. The sine of π times n/3 is zero whenever n is a multiple of 3.

options.text: None; only a square wave has missing harmonics
options.explanation: Any width that is a simple fraction makes some harmonics vanish.

options.text: Harmonics 1, 2 and 3 only
options.explanation: The fundamental is never zero for widths between 0 and 1; here its sine factor is about 0.87.

questions.workedExample:
Substitute the third harmonic first:

```formula
A_3 ∝ |sin(π × 3 × 1/3)| / 3
A_3 ∝ |sin(π)| / 3 = 0
where
A_3: the amplitude of the 3rd harmonic
∝: is proportional to
|x|: absolute value
sin: the sine function; the sine of π radians (half a cycle) is exactly 0
π: pi, about 3.14159
In words: because 3 × 1/3 is a whole number, the 3rd harmonic vanishes.
```

For one-third width, the first two sine factors are about +0.87, the third is zero, the fourth and fifth are about −0.87, and the sixth is zero. Magnitude ignores those signs. The zeros repeat at every third harmonic, which is why changing width moves spectral notches.

lessons.title: Measuring harmonics with an FFT
lessons.body:
## Check it with numpy

The roadmap asks you to compare spectra with an existing analysis tool rather than writing an FFT. numpy's `rfft` computes the discrete Fourier transform of a real signal.

The FFT reports the signal's content in a row of evenly spaced frequency slots called **bins**. Their spacing, and which bin holds a given frequency, follow from the sample rate and the number of samples analysed:

```formula
Δf = f_s / N
k = f / Δf = (fN) / f_s
Δf = 48000 Hz / 48000 = 1 Hz
where
Δf: delta f, the spacing between neighbouring bins, in hertz (Hz)
f_s: the sample rate, in Hz, here 48,000
N: the number of samples analysed, here 48,000 (one second)
k: the bin index (position in the output array) that holds frequency f
f: the frequency you want to look up, in Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: the bins are the sample rate divided by the analysis length apart; analyse one second and they are exactly 1 Hz apart, so bin number equals frequency in hertz.
```

This is **coherent sampling**: make the test components complete whole cycles in the capture. A useful trick follows: analyse exactly **one second** at an **integer** frequency. Then the FFT bins are exactly 1 Hz apart and every harmonic lands exactly on a bin, so there is no **spectral leakage** (energy smearing into neighbouring bins) to worry about. Half a second (24,000 samples) would give 2 Hz bins, so 300 Hz would be in bin 150.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f0 = 48000, 100
n = np.arange(fs)                # 1 s
p = (f0 * n / fs) % 1.0          # phase
waves = {
  "saw": 2 * p - 1,
  "square": np.where(p < 0.5, 1.0, -1.0),
  "tri": 1 - 4 * np.abs(p - 0.5),
}
for name, x in waves.items():
    # Peak amplitudes of interior real bins.
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / len(x)
    # Compare seven harmonics to the first.
    amps = X[f0 * np.arange(1, 8)]  # bin=Hz
    print(name, np.round(amps / amps[0], 3))
```

Output (harmonics 1 to 7, relative to the fundamental):

```
saw [1. 0.5 0.333 0.25 0.2 0.167 0.143]
square [1. 0. 0.333 0. 0.2 0. 0.143]
tri [1. 0. 0.111 0. 0.04 0. 0.02]
```

(Spacing tidied to fit; values unchanged.) The inverse-harmonic-number, odd-only and reciprocal-square harmonic patterns appear to the displayed precision. These are sampled naive waveforms, so small discretisation and folded-harmonic effects remain; this experiment does not prove exact band-limiting. The absolute fundamental amplitudes come out as 0.6366, 1.2732 and 0.8106, matching the leading factors of the three series above.

Note the scaling: `rfft` returns sums, not amplitudes. For a coherent real sine in an interior positive-frequency bin, multiply its magnitude by twice the reciprocal of the sample count. Do not double DC or the Nyquist endpoint, which do not have separate negative-frequency partners:

```formula
A = 2 × |X[k]| / N
|X[k]| = (NA) / 2 = 48000 × 0.5 / 2 = 12000
where
A: the amplitude (peak height) of the sine at bin k
X[k]: the complex number the FFT returns for bin k
k: the integer interior positive-frequency bin index; neither DC nor the Nyquist endpoint
|X[k]|: its magnitude (size), ignoring phase
N: the number of samples analysed, here 48,000
2: accounts for a real sine's energy being split equally between a positive and a negative frequency
In words: divide the raw bin magnitude by half the number of samples to get the sine's amplitude.
```

So one second of a 0.5-amplitude sine gives a raw magnitude of 12,000, and 2 × 12,000 / 48,000 brings it back to 0.5. For non-coherent frequencies or real recordings, a window such as `np.hanning` reduces sidelobe leakage while broadening peaks. Correct for its coherent gain if estimating amplitudes. Finite recordings and modulated sounds need a measurement method matched to the question.

## Key takeaways

- Bin spacing depends on analysis length, not just sample rate.
- Coherent steady test tones avoid leakage; windowing changes the measurement trade-off.
- Double interior positive-frequency magnitudes only when converting a real tone to peak amplitude.

## Further reading

- [Real FFT — NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)
- [FFT definitions and normalisation — NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.fft.html)
- [Spectrum analysis windows — Julius O. Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/Spectrum_Analysis_Windows.html)

questions.prompt: You run `np.fft.rfft` on **24,000** samples recorded at 48 kHz. Which output index holds the 300 Hz component?

options.explanation: That's true only when the analysis is exactly one second long (1 Hz bins). Here the bins are 2 Hz apart.
That would be the case with 2 seconds of audio (0.5 Hz bins). Half a second gives wider bins.
Correct. The bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the number of samples, 48,000 / 24,000 = 2 Hz, so 300 Hz is at index 300 / 2 = 150.
That is N/2, the index of the Nyquist frequency (24 kHz).

questions.workedExample:
```formula
Δf = f_s / N
Δf = 48000 Hz / 24000 = 2 Hz
k = f / Δf
k = 300 Hz / 2 Hz = 150
where
Δf: delta f, the spacing between FFT bins, in hertz (Hz)
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 samples per second
N: the number of samples analysed, 24,000 (half a second)
k: the index of the bin holding frequency f
f: the frequency to find, 300 Hz
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: bins are the sample rate divided by the number of samples apart, so the index is the frequency divided by that spacing.
```

This is why the lesson uses exactly one second: the spacing is 1 Hz, so indices equal hertz.

questions.prompt: You analyse exactly one second (48,000 samples) of a 1 kHz sine with amplitude 0.5. What raw magnitude does `abs(np.fft.rfft(x))[1000]` return, before any scaling?

options.explanation: That is the value *after* scaling by twice the reciprocal of the sample count. The raw FFT is an unnormalised sum.
That would be the magnitude for amplitude 1.0 (half the sample count). With amplitude 0.5 it is half that.
That is the number of samples; a sine's magnitude is split across positive and negative frequencies, so it's half the sample count times the amplitude.
Correct. The raw magnitude is the number of samples times the amplitude, halved: 48,000 × 0.5 / 2 = 12,000. Multiplying by 2 / 48,000 recovers 0.5.

questions.workedExample:
1. The DFT sums all the samples, so a sine's magnitude grows in proportion to how many samples there are.
2. A real sine's energy is shared between a positive-frequency and a negative-frequency bin, so each gets half:

```formula
|X[k]| = (NA) / 2
|X[k]| = 48000 × 0.5 / 2 = 12000
A = 2 × |X[k]| / N = 0.5
where
|X[k]|: the raw magnitude the FFT returns at bin k (here k = 1000, the 1 kHz bin)
N: the number of samples, 48,000
A: the sine's amplitude, 0.5
2: accounts for the split between positive and negative frequencies
In words: the raw bin is the amplitude times half the number of samples, so multiplying by 2/N recovers the amplitude.
```

So the raw value is **12,000**, and scaling by twice the reciprocal of the sample count gives back **0.5**.

questions.prompt: A 1 kHz sawtooth is generated at a 48 kHz sample rate. How many of its harmonics (including the fundamental) lie **below** the 24 kHz Nyquist frequency?

options.explanation: The 24th harmonic is at 24 kHz exactly, which is not *below* Nyquist.
Correct. Harmonics are at 1, 2, ..., 23 kHz below Nyquist. The 24th sits exactly on it and higher ones are above it.
That would be the count for odd harmonics only (a square), and even then it's 12 below 24 kHz: 1, 3, ..., 23.

options.text: Infinitely many
options.explanation: The ideal saw has infinitely many harmonics, but the question asks how many fit below Nyquist.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
k f_0 < f_s / 2
k × 1000 Hz < 48000 Hz / 2
k < 24
where
k: the harmonic number; harmonic k is at k × f_0
f_0: the fundamental frequency, 1000 Hz
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz
f_s / 2: the Nyquist frequency, 24,000 Hz
<: strictly less than
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: a harmonic fits only if it is below half the sample rate, so k can be 1 up to 23.
```

That is **23 harmonics**.

A Nyquist-frequency sinusoid needs special endpoint/phase treatment, and frequencies above it are not uniquely representable; the next lesson shows what happens if a naive oscillator generates it anyway (aliasing).

questions.prompt: You FFT a recording of your synth at 440 Hz and the peaks look smeared across many bins, unlike the lesson's clean output. Which are valid explanations or remedies? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smearing proves the oscillator is aliasing
options.explanation: Smearing alone does not establish aliasing. A stationary coherent naive tone can show discrete folded components, while changing frequency and finite-window leakage can spread both wanted and aliased components.

options.text: If the note has an envelope or vibrato, the spectrum genuinely changes during the window
options.explanation: Correct. A time-varying sound can't produce one sharp spectrum; analyse shorter windows or a steady section.

options.text: Apply a window such as `np.hanning` before the FFT to reduce sidelobe spectral leakage
options.explanation: Correct. Windowing tapers the ends of the segment, trading slightly wider peaks for much lower spectral leakage.

options.text: Multiply the FFT output by twice the reciprocal of the sample count to remove the smearing
options.explanation: That scaling converts magnitudes to amplitudes; it doesn't change the shape of the spectrum.

options.text: 440 Hz over your analysis length is not a whole number of cycles, so energy leaks into neighbouring bins
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson's trick (one second, integer Hz) puts every harmonic exactly on a bin. Otherwise you get spectral leakage.

questions.workedExample:
Separate *measurement* effects from *signal* effects:

1. Spectral leakage: non-integer cycles in the window. Remedy: window, or choose the length to fit whole cycles.
2. Time variation: envelopes and vibrato spread energy. Remedy: analyse a steady segment.
3. For coherent stationary tests, aliases can appear as extra discrete bins; modulated aliases and windowing can also spread energy. Do not diagnose from smearing alone.
4. twice the reciprocal of the sample count scaling only changes units.

lessons.title: Phase alignment and peak headroom
lessons.body:
## Equal magnitudes can hide different shapes

Two waves can have identical magnitude spectra but different shapes. Build a 39-harmonic saw-like tone twice: once with all harmonics in sine phase, once all in cosine phase.

```python
import numpy as np

fs, f0 = 48000, 100
t = np.arange(fs) / fs

def build(phase):
    x = np.zeros(fs)
    for n in range(1, 40):   # 39 harmonics
        # Each harmonic has inverse-number
        # gain.
        x += np.sin(2*np.pi*n*f0*t
                    + phase) / n
    return x


# Same amplitudes; change only starting
# phase.
for ph in (0.0, np.pi / 2):  # sin vs cos
    x = build(ph)
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / fs
    print(np.round(X[[100, 200, 300]], 3),
          round(np.abs(x).max(), 2))
```

```
[1.    0.5   0.333] 1.81
[1.    0.5   0.333] 4.25
```

Same harmonic amplitudes, but the cosine-phase version has a peak 2.3 times higher, because all its harmonics reach their crests together at the start of each cycle. In decibels:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(P_2 / P_1)
ΔL = 20 log_10(4.25 / 1.81) ≈ 7.4 dB
where
ΔL: delta L, the difference in peak level, in decibels (dB)
P_1: the peak of the sine-phase version, 1.81
P_2: the peak of the cosine-phase version, 4.25
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: lining up the harmonics' crests raised the peak by about 7.4 dB without changing any harmonic's amplitude.
```

The experiment proves equal harmonic magnitudes, not equal perception. Human studies of harmonic complexes show that phase differences can be audible, with sensitivity depending on harmonic resolution, fundamental frequency and listening conditions. Listen if timbre matters; do not use a magnitude FFT as proof that two tones must sound identical. Your **headroom** does not care what it sounds like: the peak is what clips. Filters change phases, which is one reason a filtered signal can peak higher than its input.

For a changing note, the harmonic levels and phases can evolve during the attack and decay. One static magnitude spectrum cannot describe all that articulation; the next unit returns to this broader meaning of timbre.

## Key takeaways

- Equal magnitude spectra can have different time-domain peaks.
- Phase changes can consume headroom even when the steady-state RMS is unchanged.

## Further reading

- [FFT definitions and normalisation — NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/routines.fft.html)
- [mdft](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/)
- [Phase discrimination in harmonic complexes — Drennan and colleagues](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2536810/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about spectra and timbre are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two steady harmonic tones with equal magnitude spectra can still sound different because harmonic phase can be audible.
options.explanation: Correct. Phase changes temporal fine structure, and listener studies show it can be discriminated under suitable conditions. Equal spectral magnitudes alone do not establish perceptual identity.

options.text: Two waveforms with identical harmonic magnitudes but different phases can look very different on a scope
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson's sine-phase vs cosine-phase example had the same spectrum but peaks of 1.81 vs 4.25.

options.text: Sharper waveform corners need fewer harmonics
options.explanation: The reverse: sharp corners and jumps need many high harmonics.

options.text: A sound's timbre is fully described by one static magnitude spectrum
options.explanation: Timbre also depends on how the spectrum changes over time (attack, decay of harmonics), which is why envelopes and filters matter.

options.text: The pitch we hear for a saw is normally its fundamental frequency
options.explanation: Correct. Harmonics at integer multiples fuse into one note at f0.

questions.workedExample:
Check each against the lesson:

- Phase changes shape and peak: **true**.
- Phase can affect the perception of steady harmonic complexes: **true**.
- A harmonic saw is normally heard near its fundamental: **true**.
- A static magnitude spectrum fully describes timbre: **false**; evolution over time matters.
- Sharper corners require fewer harmonics: **false**.

questions.prompt: You normalise a patch so a sine-phase additive saw peaks at 0.9. You then add a phase-shifting effect that leaves every harmonic's *amplitude* unchanged, and the output starts clipping. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The effect added new harmonics above Nyquist, which alias and raise the level
options.explanation: A phase-only change adds no new frequencies, so nothing new can alias.

options.text: The phase shift lined up harmonic peaks more closely, raising the waveform's peak even though the spectrum magnitudes are unchanged
options.explanation: Correct. Peak level depends on how harmonics align in time. The lesson saw 1.81 vs 4.25 for the same spectrum (about 7.4 dB).

options.text: Phase shifts always add 3 dB of gain
options.explanation: There is no fixed gain; an all-pass phase change leaves each sine's amplitude the same. The *peak* depends on alignment.

options.text: The FFT shows the same spectrum, so clipping must come from a bug elsewhere
options.explanation: Same magnitude spectrum does not mean same peak. This is a real effect, not necessarily a bug.

questions.workedExample:
1. Magnitudes unchanged, so the RMS (overall energy) is unchanged.
2. Peak = how the harmonics' crests coincide. A phase shift can align more of them.
3. In the lesson, aligning all 39 harmonics (cosine phase) took the peak from 1.81 to 4.25:

```formula
ΔL = 20 log_10(P_2 / P_1)
ΔL = 20 log_10(4.25 / 1.81) ≈ 7.4 dB
where
ΔL: delta L, the rise in peak level, in decibels (dB)
P_1: the sine-phase peak, 1.81
P_2: the cosine-phase peak, 4.25
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the same harmonics, lined up, peak about 7.4 dB higher.
```

4. So a 0.9 peak could become well above 1.0 and clip.

Practical lesson: leave headroom after any filter or phase-altering stage, and measure peaks, not just spectra.

lessons.title: Gibbs ripple and evolving timbre
lessons.body:
## Gibbs ripple

Adding up a finite number of harmonics never quite produces a perfect corner. A square wave built from odd harmonics overshoots each jump by about 9% of the jump size, in the limit of a large Fourier-series term count. A particular short finite sum differs slightly:

```formula
P ≈ 1 + 0.09 × J
P ≈ 1 + 0.09 × 2 ≈ 1.18
where
P: the peak value of the band-limited square, which ideally would be 1
J: the size of the jump, from −1 to +1, so 2
0.09: the Gibbs overshoot, about 9% (more precisely 8.95%) of the jump
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a ±1 square made from a finite number of harmonics peaks at about 1.18, so it needs about 1.4 dB more headroom than the ideal square.
```

This is the **Gibbs phenomenon**. It matters later: a hard Fourier truncation of a square or saw shows this ripple even with every retained harmonic below Nyquist. Other smoothing windows and approximate oscillators can change the overshoot, so it is not a mandatory 18% peak for every anti-aliased implementation.

## Timbre is more than the static spectrum

The spectrum explains why waveforms differ, but real timbre also depends on how the spectrum **changes over time**. A piano's high harmonics die faster than its fundamental; a brass note gets brighter as it gets louder. That is why synths pair oscillators with filters, envelopes and modulation, which change the spectrum while the note plays. The DSP learning objectives ask you to describe a target sound in exactly these terms: pitch, spectrum, envelope and modulation.

## Key takeaways

- Limiting an ideal jump to finitely many Fourier terms creates ripple and overshoot.
- More terms narrow the overshoot region; allow peak headroom.
- Timbre includes changes over time as well as a steady magnitude spectrum.

## Further reading

- [Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF](https://dlmf.nist.gov/6.16)
- [Blofeld user manual — Waldorf](https://downloads.waldorfmusic.com/cloud/index.php/s/32zdTsdYcRSX9eE/download)

questions.prompt: You generate a properly band-limited square wave (many odd harmonics, scaled by 4/π so the flat parts sit at ±1). Your output stage clips at ±1.0. Roughly what gain should you apply to avoid clipping on its own?

options.text: 1.0, because the square only reaches ±1
options.explanation: The band-limited square overshoots its edges by about 9% of the 2-unit jump (Gibbs), peaking near ±1.18.

options.text: About 0.5, because a square has twice the energy of a sine
options.explanation: Energy is not what clips; the peak is. 0.5 is much more cut than needed.

options.text: About 0.85
options.explanation: Correct. The Gibbs overshoot gives peaks of about 1.18, and 1 / 1.18 ≈ 0.85 brings them to 1.0. In practice you'd go lower still for headroom.

options.text: About 0.64 (2/π)
options.explanation: 2/π relates to the saw's fundamental amplitude; it isn't the right factor for the square's Gibbs peak.

questions.workedExample:
1. Gibbs phenomenon: a finite sum of harmonics overshoots a jump by about 9% of the jump.
2. Work out the peak, then the gain that brings it back to 1.0:

```formula
P ≈ 1 + 0.09 × J
P ≈ 1 + 0.09 × 2 ≈ 1.18
G = 1 / P ≈ 1 / 1.18 ≈ 0.85
where
P: the peak of the band-limited square
J: the jump size, from −1 to +1, so 2
0.09: the Gibbs overshoot, about 9% of the jump
G: the gain (multiplier) that brings the peak to exactly 1.0
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the edges overshoot to about 1.18, so the approximate boundary is about 0.848. A literal gain of 0.85 can still exceed unity slightly, so use a lower gain such as 0.84 for margin.
```

Summing odd harmonics up to the 39th, or up to the 199th, give peaks close to 1.179, with finite-term and sampling differences.

The overshoot doesn't shrink as you add harmonics; it just narrows.

lessons.title: Where naive oscillator harmonics fold
lessons.body:
The earlier harmonic-pattern unit showed that a sawtooth has harmonics at every multiple of its fundamental, forever. A digital system can only represent frequencies below half its sample rate (the **Nyquist frequency**: 24 kHz at a 48 kHz sample rate). Module 1 covered what happens to anything above: it **aliases**, folding back to a different frequency.

The naive oscillator from the oscillator units, `2.0 * p - 1.0`, samples an ideal saw directly. It therefore contains all those impossible harmonics, and they fold back into the audible band. This lesson puts numbers on the problem and shows how real synths solve it.

## Where the harmonics go

Take a high-ish note: 1245 Hz (close to D#6) at a 48 kHz sample rate. Nyquist is 24 kHz, so harmonics 1 to 19 (up to 23,655 Hz) are fine. Harmonic 20 is at 24,900 Hz and folds back. A component above Nyquist lands at its distance from the nearest whole multiple of the sample rate:

```formula
f_h = h f_0
f_a = |f_h − k f_s|
h = 20: |24900 − 48000| = 23100 Hz
h = 21: |26145 − 48000| = 21855 Hz
h = 31: |38595 − 48000| = 9405 Hz
h = 38: |47310 − 48000| = 690 Hz
h = 39: |48555 − 48000| = 555 Hz
where
f_h: the frequency of harmonic h, in hertz (Hz)
h: the harmonic number, 1, 2, 3...
f_0: the fundamental frequency (the note), here 1245 Hz
f_a: the alias: the frequency the harmonic actually appears at after sampling, in Hz
|x|: absolute value: x without its sign, so a distance is never negative
k: the whole number that makes k × f_s as close as possible to f_h (here k = 1, since all these harmonics lie between 24 and 72 kHz)
f_s: the sample rate, here 48,000 Hz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: sampling cannot tell a frequency apart from one that is a whole multiple of the sample rate away, so each harmonic above Nyquist shows up at its distance from the nearest multiple of the sample rate.
```

The table tracks each isolated ideal source harmonic using its reciprocal-harmonic-number amplitude. Several harmonics can fold to one sampled frequency and add or cancel, so these levels are not guaranteed total FFT-bin amplitudes:

```formula
L = 20 log_10(1 / h)
L = 20 log_10(1 / 31) ≈ −29.8 dB
where
L: the level relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB)
h: the harmonic number, here 31
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to to get the number
dB: decibels
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the 31st harmonic of a saw is 1/31 of the fundamental's amplitude, about 30 dB quieter.
```

| Harmonic | Lands at | Level (the reciprocal of harmonic number) |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 23,100 Hz | −26.0 dB |
| 31 | 9,405 Hz | −29.8 dB |
| 38 | 690 Hz | −31.6 dB |
| 39 | 555 Hz | −31.8 dB |

Two things make this bad:

- **The aliases are not harmonic.** 9,405 Hz and 690 Hz are not multiples of 1245 Hz, so they sound like dissonant, metallic tones rather than brightness.
- **They move the wrong way.** Bend the pitch up and a real harmonic rises, but a folded one can *fall*. Pitch sweeps produce the tell-tale "birdie" whistles moving against the note.

A component 30 dB below the fundamental can be audible when it is poorly masked, but audibility depends on the sound, listener and playback level; that number alone is not an audibility threshold. Low notes suffer less, because their harmonics are already weak (the reciprocal of harmonic number is small) by the time they reach Nyquist.

> [!note] Why square waves are no better
> The naive square also has slowly decaying odd harmonics, so it can alias strongly. The exact folded levels differ from a saw. A naive triangle is much better (the reciprocal of harmonic number squared falls faster), and a fixed sine strictly below Nyquist has no upper harmonics to fold. Pitch modulation, clipping or an above-Nyquist sine requires separate analysis. The problem is **discontinuities**: a periodic jump requires harmonics extending to arbitrarily high frequencies.

## Key takeaways

- Naive sharp waveforms contain harmonics beyond Nyquist.
- Folded components can be inharmonic and move down while pitch moves up.

## Further reading

- [Aliasing — Julius O. Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/mdft/Aliasing_Sampled_Signals.html)
- [Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)

questions.prompt: What feature of a naive sawtooth (`2*p - 1`) is the root cause of its aliasing?

options.text: Its straight rising segment
options.explanation: A straight ramp on its own is smooth; it's the reset at the end of each ramp that causes trouble.

options.text: Its instantaneous jump from +1 to −1, requiring harmonics extending to arbitrarily high frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. A periodic discontinuity needs infinitely many high harmonics. Sampling it directly folds above-Nyquist contributions back down; they can add or cancel at coincident sampled frequencies.

options.text: Its amplitude of ±1
options.explanation: Scaling the wave changes the level of the aliases, not whether they exist.

options.text: Using floating point instead of integers
options.explanation: An integer implementation of the same naive wave aliases identically. It's a sampling problem, not a number-format one.

questions.workedExample:
1. Lesson 3: sharp features need many high harmonics; an ideal saw jump requires arbitrarily high harmonics, with inverse-harmonic-number amplitudes.
2. Anything above half the sample rate (the Nyquist frequency) cannot be represented, so it folds back (module 1).
3. The ramp is harmless; correct the jump (BLEP) or never create it (additive, wavetables) and unwanted folding can be prevented or reduced, depending on the algorithm. A short PolyBLEP is approximate, and a time-varying waveform needs separate sideband analysis.

questions.prompt: A naive saw plays at 2,500 Hz with a 48 kHz sample rate. Where does its ideal 19th-harmonic contribution fold, and what is that source harmonic’s level relative to the ideal fundamental?

options.explanation: 47.5 kHz can't exist at a 48 kHz sample rate; it must fold below 24 kHz.

options.text: It is simply removed because it is above Nyquist
options.explanation: Nothing removes it: a naive oscillator samples the ideal wave, so the harmonic folds back instead of disappearing.

options.text: 500 Hz at about −25.6 dB
options.explanation: Correct. The ideal 19th harmonic is 47,500 Hz, which folds to 500 Hz. Its source amplitude is one nineteenth of the ideal fundamental, about minus 25.6 dB. Other harmonics can fold to the same bin, so this is not a prediction of the total sampled FFT-bin level.

options.text: 23,500 Hz at about −25.6 dB
options.explanation: That would be reflecting around Nyquist from 24,500 Hz. Measure the distance to the nearest multiple of the sample rate instead: 47,500 is close to 48,000, so it lands near 0 Hz.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
f_h = h f_0
f_h = 19 × 2500 Hz = 47500 Hz
f_a = |f_h − k f_s|
f_a = |47500 − 48000| = 500 Hz
L = 20 log_10(1 / h)
L = 20 log_10(1 / 19) ≈ −25.6 dB
where
f_h: the harmonic's frequency, in hertz (Hz)
h: the harmonic number
f_0: the note's fundamental frequency, in Hz
f_a: the alias: where the harmonic actually appears after sampling, in Hz
|x|: absolute value: x without its sign
k: the whole number that puts k × f_s nearest to f_h
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz
L: the level relative to the fundamental, in decibels (dB), from the saw's 1/h amplitude rule
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
≈: approximately equal to
dB: decibels
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: the 19th harmonic folds to 500 Hz, about 26 dB below the fundamental.
```

A 500 Hz tone under a 2.5 kHz note is not a multiple of it, so it sounds like a clashing low whistle.

This tracks one ideal source harmonic. Other folded harmonics can coincide and add or cancel, so measure the combined sampled FFT-bin amplitude separately.

questions.prompt: Why are aliased components from a naive oscillator so much more objectionable than the same amount of extra brightness?

options.text: They are louder than the fundamental
options.explanation: Usually they are well below it (around −26 to −32 dB in the lesson's example). Level isn't the main issue.

options.text: They only occur in square waves
options.explanation: Other naive sharp waveforms alias too. A fixed sine below Nyquist has no upper harmonics to fold; above-Nyquist or modulated sines need separate checks.

options.text: They can be inharmonic and can move in the opposite direction when the pitch changes
options.explanation: Correct. Folded components aren't multiples of the fundamental, so they clash, and on a pitch sweep some fall while the note rises.

options.text: They increase the DC offset
options.explanation: Aliases can land at DC as well as other frequencies. A DC shift alone does not explain the characteristic moving inharmonic whistles in the question.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
f_h = k f_0
f_a = |k f_0 − m f_s|
where
f_h: a real harmonic's frequency, in hertz (Hz)
k: the harmonic number
f_0: the note's fundamental frequency, in Hz
f_a: the alias frequency, in Hz
|x|: absolute value: x without its sign
m: the whole number that puts m × f_s nearest to the harmonic
f_s: the sample rate, in Hz
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: real harmonics rise with the note, but when a harmonic sits just below a multiple of the sample rate, raising the note shrinks the gap, so the alias falls.
```

So a sweep up produces whistles sweeping down ('birdies'). That motion and inharmonicity can make aliases at −30 dB audible when masking and playback conditions permit; the number is not a universal hearing threshold.

questions.prompt: A naive saw at 2,000 Hz (48 kHz sample rate) is bent up to 2,010 Hz. Its 20th harmonic folds back. What happens to that alias?

options.text: It rises by 10 Hz
options.explanation: That treats the alias like the fundamental. The 20th harmonic moves 20 times as far, and the folding reverses its direction.

options.text: It falls by 200 Hz, from 8,000 to 7,800 Hz
options.explanation: Correct. 20 × 2000 = 40,000 → 48,000 − 40,000 = 8,000 Hz. 20 × 2010 = 40,200 → 7,800 Hz. The note goes up while the alias goes down.

options.text: It rises by 200 Hz, from 8,000 to 8,200 Hz
options.explanation: The harmonic rises by 200 Hz, but because it's folded around 48 kHz, its alias falls.

options.text: It stays at 8,000 Hz
options.explanation: Every component moves when the pitch changes; only the direction differs.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
f_a = |h f_0 − k f_s|
f_0 = 2000 Hz: |40000 − 48000| = 8000 Hz
f_0 = 2010 Hz: |40200 − 48000| = 7800 Hz
where
h: the harmonic number
f_0: the note's fundamental frequency, in Hz
f_a: the alias: where the harmonic actually appears after sampling, in Hz
|x|: absolute value: x without its sign
k: the whole number that puts k × f_s nearest to the harmonic's frequency (here 1)
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: the 20th harmonic rises from 40,000 to 40,200 Hz, closer to 48,000 Hz, so its alias falls from 8,000 to 7,800 Hz.
```

Harmonic +200 Hz, alias −200 Hz. This counter-motion is why pitch sweeps on naive oscillators sound so wrong.

lessons.title: Harmonic limits and wavetable ranges
lessons.body:
## Established fixes

There is no free lunch. Each method trades CPU, memory, latency or flexibility.

### 1. Additive synthesis

Sum only the harmonics below Nyquist. How many is that? The largest whole number whose harmonic stays strictly below half the sample rate:

```formula
H = ⌈(f_s / 2) / f_0⌉ − 1
H = ⌈24000 / 1245⌉ − 1 = ⌈19.3⌉ − 1 = 19
H = ⌈24000 / 50⌉ − 1 = 480 − 1 = 479
where
H: the number of harmonics that fit below Nyquist (the highest usable harmonic number)
⌈x⌉: the ceiling of x: x rounded up to the next whole number; a whole number stays as it is
f_s: the sample rate, here 48,000 Hz
f_s / 2: the Nyquist frequency, here 24,000 Hz
f_0: the note's fundamental frequency, in hertz (Hz)
In words: divide Nyquist by the note's frequency, round up, and subtract one, so that a harmonic landing exactly on Nyquist is excluded.
```

For this note that is harmonics 1 to 19. The result is perfectly band-limited by construction. The cost is one sine per harmonic per sample: a 50 Hz note at 48 kHz has 479 harmonics below Nyquist. Fine offline, expensive for a polyphonic synth on a microcontroller.

### 2. Band-limited wavetables (mipmaps)

Precompute single-cycle tables using additive synthesis, offline. Keep several versions: one per octave (say), each containing only the harmonics that stay below Nyquist for the **highest** note that table will play. At playback, choose the table for the current pitch and read it with a phase accumulator and interpolation. The same counting rule sets each table's harmonic limit, using the highest note the table serves:

```formula
H = ⌈(f_s / 2) / f_top⌉ − 1
f_top = 2000 Hz: ⌈24000 / 2000⌉ − 1 = 11
f_top = 1000 Hz: ⌈24000 / 1000⌉ − 1 = 23
f_top = 500 Hz: ⌈24000 / 500⌉ − 1 = 47
where
H: the highest harmonic the table may contain
⌈x⌉: the ceiling of x: rounded up to a whole number (a whole number stays as it is)
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz, so f_s / 2 = 24,000 Hz
f_top: the highest note the table will play, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: each octave lower, the table can hold about twice as many harmonics.
```

This is cheap per sample and works for any waveform, which is why wavetable synths use it. The costs are memory, a slight loss of brightness at the bottom of each table's range, and possible audible switching between tables (crossfading helps). Some designs deliberately allow harmonics that fold back *above* 20 kHz, keeping more brightness at the cost of some inaudible aliasing.

## Key takeaways

- Count harmonics strictly below Nyquist, including exact equality with Nyquist.
- Additive generation trades processing work for explicit spectral control; tables trade memory for playback cost.

## Further reading

- [Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)
- [Additive synthesis — Julius O. Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/pasp/Additive_Synthesis.html)

questions.prompt: You build mipmapped saw tables at a 48 kHz sample rate with no aliasing allowed. One table serves notes up to 3.5 kHz. What is the highest harmonic it may contain?

options.explanation: Correct. Each harmonic of a 3.5 kHz note must stay below 24 kHz: 24,000 / 3,500 ≈ 6.86, so the 6th is the highest (it is at 21 kHz; the 7th would be 24.5 kHz).
That uses the full 48 kHz sample rate instead of half of it: 48,000 / 3,500 ≈ 13.7. Harmonics up to 45.5 kHz would alias badly.
24 kHz is exactly Nyquist for a 1 kHz top note; strictly below Nyquist would allow only 23 harmonics there.

options.text: As many as you like; tables are band-limited automatically
options.explanation: Tables only become band-limited if you build them that way, with additive synthesis limited by the table's highest note.

questions.workedExample:
Rule: every harmonic of the table's highest note must be below Nyquist.

```formula
H = ⌈(f_s / 2) / f_top⌉ − 1
H = ⌈24000 / 3500⌉ − 1 = ⌈6.86⌉ − 1 = 6
6 × 3500 Hz = 21000 Hz
7 × 3500 Hz = 24500 Hz
where
H: the highest harmonic the table may contain
⌈x⌉: the ceiling of x: rounded up to a whole number
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz; f_s / 2 is Nyquist, 24,000 Hz
f_top: the highest note the table serves, 3,500 Hz
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: the 6th harmonic (21 kHz) fits below 24 kHz; the 7th (24.5 kHz) would not.
```

Lower notes in the same table lose a little brightness because they could have used more harmonics. That's the mipmap trade-off.

questions.prompt: You consider additive saws for an 8-voice synth at 48 kHz whose lowest note is 55 Hz. In the worst case (all voices on the lowest note), roughly how many sine evaluations per output sample does that need?

options.text: About 3,500
options.explanation: Correct. 24,000 / 55 ≈ 436 harmonics per voice, × 8 voices ≈ 3,488 sines per sample, i.e. over 167 million per second.

options.text: About 440
options.explanation: That's one voice. Polyphony multiplies the cost.

options.text: About 7,000
options.explanation: That uses the full 48 kHz sample rate as the limit instead of the 24 kHz Nyquist frequency.

options.text: 8, one per voice
options.explanation: That would be a sine oscillator per voice; a saw needs every harmonic below Nyquist.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
H = ⌈(f_s / 2) / f_0⌉ − 1
H = ⌈24000 / 55⌉ − 1 = ⌈436.4⌉ − 1
H = 436
S = H × V = 436 × 8 = 3488
S × f_s = 3488 × 48000 Hz ≈ 1.67e8
where
H: harmonics per voice below Nyquist
⌈x⌉: the ceiling of x: rounded up to a whole number
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 samples per second; f_s / 2 is Nyquist, 24,000 Hz
f_0: the lowest note, 55 Hz
S: sine evaluations per output sample
V: the number of voices, 8
Hz: hertz, per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 436 sines per voice times 8 voices is about 3,500 sines every sample, or about 167 million a second.
```

That's why additive is rarely used for plain saws on small hardware, and why tables or PolyBLEP are preferred.

questions.prompt: At a 48 kHz sample rate you decide aliases are acceptable if they land at or above 20 kHz (beyond most listeners' hearing). For a mipmap table whose highest note is 2 kHz, what's the highest harmonic you can now keep?

options.explanation: 12 reaches Nyquist exactly at 2 kHz; the strict below-Nyquist limit is 11. The relaxed rule permits more.
Correct. A harmonic between 24 and 48 kHz folds to 48 kHz minus its frequency. For that to be at least 20 kHz the harmonic must be at most 28 kHz; 28,000 / 2,000 = 14.
That limits harmonics to 20 kHz itself, which is stricter than needed.
Harmonic 24 reaches 48 kHz and can alias to DC at the top note and low frequencies nearby. DC itself is not an audible tone, but is undesirable.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
f_a = f_s − f_h
f_s − f_h ≥ 20000 Hz
f_h ≤ 48000 Hz − 20000 Hz = 28000 Hz
H = 28000 Hz / 2000 Hz = 14
where
f_a: the alias frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_s: the sample rate, 48,000 Hz
f_h: a harmonic's frequency, between 24 and 48 kHz, in Hz
≥, ≤: at least; at most
H: the highest harmonic of the 2 kHz top note that may be kept
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: harmonics up to 28 kHz fold to 20 kHz or above, and 28 kHz is the 14th harmonic of a 2 kHz note.
```

You gain three extra (relative to a strict 11-harmonic table) harmonics' brightness for the lowest notes in that table, and the aliases that do occur sit at 20–24 kHz. It is a deliberate engineering trade-off; check it suits your output chain (some listeners and equipment may still respond up there).

lessons.title: Oversampling, BLIT and BLEP methods
lessons.body:
### 3. Oversampling

Run the naive oscillator at a multiple of the sample rate (say 4× or 8×), low-pass filter, then discard samples (decimate). Aliases still occur, but they fold around the higher Nyquist and most of their energy is filtered out. Simple to reason about, costly in CPU, and the decimation filter must be good.

### 4. BLIT: band-limited impulse train

Stilson and Smith (CCRMA, 1996) generate a band-limited train of impulses using a closed-form formula, then **integrate** it to get a saw (or integrate a bipolar impulse train for a square). It's elegant and accurate, though the integrators need care to avoid DC drift.

### 5. BLEP and PolyBLEP: correct the jumps

Insight: a saw is smooth everywhere *except* at its jump. Aliasing comes from the jumps. So generate the naive wave, then **add a correction** around each discontinuity that approximates a suitably low-pass-smoothed step. Ideal band-limited steps have infinite support; practical finite corrections leave some residual aliasing.

- **minBLEP** (Eli Brandt, 2001) precomputes a band-limited step, makes it minimum-phase, and stores the difference from an ideal step in a table. At each jump, the oscillator adds the table, aligned to the jump's exact fractional position.
- **PolyBLEP** (Välimäki and Huovilainen, 2007) replaces the table with a tiny polynomial that only touches two samples: the one just before the jump and the one just after it. It is cheap and needs no correction lookup table, at the cost of weaker suppression than a long table.

```diagram
naive saw          PolyBLEP saw
    /|  /|             /\  /\
   / | / |            /  \/  \
  /  |/  |           /        \
 jump: 1 sample      jump spread over
 (aliases)           ~2 samples
```

## Key takeaways

- Oversampling requires filtering before decimation.
- BLIT integrates a band-limited impulse train; BLEP methods correct discontinuities.
- Finite tables and short polynomial corrections reduce rather than guarantee zero aliasing.

## Further reading

- [Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith](https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~stilti/papers/blit.pdf)
- [Hard sync without aliasing — Eli Brandt](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~eli/papers/icmc01-hardsync.pdf)
- [Antialiasing oscillators — Välimäki and Huovilainen](https://research.aalto.fi/en/publications/antialiasing-oscillators-in-subtractive-synthesis/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about band-limiting methods are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: minBLEP adds a precomputed band-limited step correction at each discontinuity
options.explanation: Correct. Brandt's method stores the difference between a minimum-phase band-limited step and an ideal step.

options.text: PolyBLEP removes all aliasing perfectly
options.explanation: It greatly reduces aliasing (about 25 dB in the lesson's test) but doesn't remove it entirely, and it slightly dulls the top octave.

options.text: Additive synthesis is exactly band-limited if you only sum harmonics below Nyquist
options.explanation: Correct. For fixed frequencies and amplitudes, the constructed sum has only the selected below-Nyquist components in exact arithmetic. Modulating them can introduce new sidebands, and numerical approximations need checking.

options.text: Mipmapped wavetables trade memory for low per-sample CPU and work for arbitrary waveforms
options.explanation: Correct. Tables are built offline; playback is a lookup and interpolation.

options.text: Oversampling needs no filter, because the aliases fold above the audible range
options.explanation: After oversampling you must low-pass filter before decimating; otherwise the content folds right back down.

questions.workedExample:
Check each method's mechanism:

| Method | Exact? | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Additive | yes | CPU |
| Mipmaps | near | memory |
| minBLEP | near | small table |
| PolyBLEP | reduced | tiny |
| Oversampling | reduced | CPU + filter |

Oversampling without a decimation filter just recreates the aliasing at the lower rate.

link.title: Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith

questions.prompt: Which methods reduce aliasing during oscillator generation or before final downsampling, rather than merely attenuating output afterwards? Select all that apply.

options.text: Switch to mipmapped band-limited wavetables
options.explanation: Correct. Each table contains only harmonics that stay below Nyquist for its note range.

options.text: Put a 10 kHz low-pass filter after the oscillator
options.explanation: A post-filter can remove aliases above 10 kHz, but cannot separate aliases below its cutoff from wanted sound. It is not prevention during generation.

options.text: Add PolyBLEP corrections at both the rising and falling edges
options.explanation: Correct. Opposite corrections smooth the two jumps and reduce their aliasing; the fixed-note test measured about 25 dB less worst off-harmonic content below 10 kHz. This is approximate suppression, not a zero-aliasing guarantee.

options.text: Turn the oscillator's output level down
options.explanation: Aliases scale with the signal; their level relative to the note doesn't change.

options.text: Run the naive oscillator 4× oversampled, low-pass filter, then decimate
options.explanation: Correct. Most folded energy lands above the original band and is removed by the decimation filter.

questions.workedExample:
Key idea: aliasing happens **at the moment of sampling**. Once a component has folded to 690 Hz, it *is* a 690 Hz component.

So the fix must act before or during generation:

- correct the jumps (PolyBLEP/minBLEP),
- never create the high harmonics (tables, additive),
- or generate at a higher rate and filter before reducing the rate (oversampling).

Filtering or gain changes afterwards can't separate aliases from the real tone.

lessons.title: A measured PolyBLEP saw experiment
lessons.body:
This is an offline NumPy experiment requiring NumPy installed in the Python environment. All subsequent NumPy experiments use the same dependency. The test is one second at a fixed integer frequency, so the FFT bins are one hertz apart. It compares this polynomial implementation, not a proof about every BLEP library or about modulated notes.

## A PolyBLEP saw in Python

The polynomial below is the widely circulated two-sample PolyBLEP (as used in Martin Finke's tutorial). Written as maths first:

```formula
y = 2p − 1 − B
B = 2u − u^2 − 1,  u = p / dt
B = u^2 + 2u + 1,  u = (p − 1) / dt
where
y: the corrected saw output sample
p: the phase, from 0 up to 1, in cycles
B: the PolyBLEP correction: use the first formula when p < dt (the sample just after the jump), the second when p > 1 − dt (the sample just before it), and B = 0 otherwise
u: how far the sample is from the jump, measured in samples: between 0 and 1 just after it, between −1 and 0 just before it
dt: the phase increment per sample (f_0 / f_s), as in the code
f_0: the note's frequency, in hertz
f_s: the sample rate, in hertz
<, >: less than, greater than
In words: away from the jump the saw is untouched; on the one sample either side of the jump, a small curve is subtracted that replaces the instant drop with a short smooth approximation with reduced aliasing, not an ideal strictly band-limited step.
```

For the numeric half-sample example, a phase of 0.05 cycles with an increment of 0.1 gives a rescaled distance of 0.5. The correction is −0.25, so the corrected sample is −0.65 rather than the naive −0.9. The question’s worked card shows the substitution. The code assumes constant positive frequency strictly below Nyquist, finite values, and one sample-loop evaluation per output sample:

```python
import numpy as np

def poly_blep(t, dt):
    # t: phase [0,1), dt: increment
    if t < dt:             # just after jump
        t = t / dt
        return t + t - t * t - 1.0
    if t > 1.0 - dt:       # just before
        t = (t - 1.0) / dt
        return t * t + t + t + 1.0
    return 0.0

def saw(f0, fs, n, blep):
    dt, p = f0 / fs, 0.0
    out = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        y = 2.0 * p - 1.0
        if blep:
            # Falling edge: subtract
            # correction.
            y -= poly_blep(p, dt)
        out[i] = y
        p += dt
        if p >= 1.0:
            p -= 1.0
    return out

fs, f0 = 48000, 1245     # 1 s: bin = 1 Hz
k = np.arange(fs // 2 + 1)

# Only multiples of f0 are wanted harmonics.
harm = (k % f0 == 0) & (k > 0)
low = (k > 0) & (k < 10000)
for blep in (False, True):
    x = saw(f0, fs, fs, blep)
    X = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2 / fs
    # Search off-harmonic bins below 10 kHz.
    alias = np.where(~harm & low, X, 0)
    w = np.argmax(alias)
    db = 20 * np.log10(alias[w] / X[f0])
    # Droop versus the ideal tenth harmonic.
    h10 = 20 * np.log10(X[10 * f0] * 10
                        / X[f0])
    print("polyblep" if blep else "naive",
          w, round(db, 1), round(h10, 1))
```

Output:

```
naive 9405 -29.8 0.0
polyblep 9405 -55.4 -1.9
```

Reading it: the strongest alias below 10 kHz is at 9,405 Hz in both cases (harmonic 31 folded), but PolyBLEP pushes it from −29.8 dB to −55.4 dB relative to the fundamental, an improvement of about 25 dB. The last column is the 10th harmonic (12,450 Hz) relative to its ideal the reciprocal of harmonic number level: PolyBLEP softens it by 1.9 dB. In the same run the 19th harmonic (23.7 kHz) was 7.6 dB low. That is PolyBLEP's trade-off: it gently dulls the very top octave while removing most of the audible aliasing.

## Key takeaways

- Evaluate the correction relative to the edge and subtract it for a falling saw edge.
- Measure residual aliases and wanted-harmonic droop together.

## Further reading

- [Oscillator implementation — DaisySP](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electro-smith/DaisySP/2c72eaf9eac5fc0dca1919d65d606da907832618/Source/Synthesis/oscillator.cpp)
- [finke](https://www.martin-finke.de/articles/audio-plugins-018-polyblep-oscillator/)
- [Real FFT — NumPy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.fft.rfft.html)

lessons.title: Pulse corrections and library oscillators
lessons.body:
The saw's jump is downwards (+1 to −1), so the correction is *subtracted*. A square has a rising jump at phase 0 and a falling one at the oscillator pulse width w, so it needs two corrections:

```formula
y = s + B(p) − B((p − w) mod 1)
where
y: the corrected pulse output sample
s: the naive pulse: +1 while p < w, otherwise −1
p: the phase, from 0 up to 1
w: the oscillator pulse width, as a fraction of the cycle (0.5 for a square)
B(x): the signed PolyBLEP step-correction function at the wrapped phase x, using the same fixed positive increment for both edges
x: the function’s dummy phase argument, from zero inclusive to one exclusive
mod: modulo, the remainder after division; (p − w) mod 1 is the phase measured from the falling edge, wrapped into 0 to 1
In words: add a correction at the rising edge and subtract one at the falling edge, each measured from its own jump.
```

This is a Python fragment using the preceding unit’s `poly_blep` function. Supply a phase, a fixed oscillator pulse width strictly between zero and one, and a positive increment below half a cycle per sample. Extremely narrow pulses and moving edges need additional validation:

```python
y = 1.0 if p < w else -1.0

# Rising edge at the start of each cycle.
y += poly_blep(p, dt)

# Falling edge measured from the duty point.
y -= poly_blep((p - w) % 1.0, dt)
```

The same fixed-frequency FFT check, at oscillator pulse widths 0.5 and 0.3, gave −55.4 dB worst off-harmonic bin below 10 kHz for the corrected version (naive: −29.8 and −28.7 dB respectively). Remember that a pulse with a width other than 0.5 also has a DC offset (a non-zero average), which you may want to remove:

```formula
DC = w(+1) + (1 − w) × (−1) = 2w − 1
DC = 2 × 0.3 − 1 = −0.4
where
DC: the average value of the pulse over one cycle
w: the oscillator pulse width, the fraction of the cycle spent at +1; the rest, 1 − w, is spent at −1
In words: the average is the time-weighted mix of +1 and −1, which is zero only for a square (w = 0.5).
```

Triangle waves have corners, not jumps. They can be corrected with a band-limited *ramp* (BLAMP), or made by integrating a PolyBLEP square with a leaky integrator, which is what DaisySP's `WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI` does.

## Using a library

You don't need to invent any of this. Source revisions checked 2026-10-16: DaisySP 2c72eaf9eac5 and PJRC Audio 3039be2773e8. These are software-library observations, not a board-revision compatibility claim; confirm your installed library before copying names:

- **DaisySP** `Oscillator` offers naive waveforms plus `WAVE_POLYBLEP_SAW`, `WAVE_POLYBLEP_SQUARE` and `WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI`.
- **Teensy Audio Library** `AudioSynthWaveform` offers `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH`, `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH_REVERSE`, `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SQUARE` and `WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_PULSE` alongside the naive ones. Its source (`synth_waveform.cpp`, class `BandLimitedWaveform`) inserts a precomputed band-limited step from a lookup table at each edge, interpolated to the edge's fractional position and spread across a window of about 32 samples (16 either side of the edge): a table-based BLEP approach, not PolyBLEP.

The roadmap exercise is exactly this lesson's experiment: generate naive and band-limited versions at a high pitch, run them through the FFT analysis, and listen to a slow upward sweep of each.

The fixed-note test also works with the actual checked DaisySP oscillator source compiled on the host: the naive saw’s strongest off-harmonic bin below 10 kHz was about −29.83 dB relative to its fundamental, versus −55.45 dB for its PolyBLEP saw. The tenth-harmonic droop was about −1.95 dB. These measurements agree closely with the offline Python implementation; they do not measure a board’s real-time capacity, output circuit or behaviour under rapidly changing pitch.

## Choosing a method

| Method | CPU | Memory | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Additive | high | low | exact; costly for low notes |
| Mipmapped tables | low | medium | any waveform |
| Oversampling | high | low | needs a good decimator |
| PolyBLEP | low | no correction table | some top-end droop |
| minBLEP | medium | small table | better suppression |

For a first subtractive voice on a microcontroller, PolyBLEP is the usual pragmatic choice.

## Key takeaways

- Pulse waves need opposite corrections at rising and falling edges.
- Non-half duty cycles have a non-zero mean.
- Inspect the exact library revision and compare its output with the naive oscillator.

## Further reading

- [Oscillator implementation — DaisySP](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/electro-smith/DaisySP/2c72eaf9eac5fc0dca1919d65d606da907832618/Source/Synthesis/oscillator.cpp)
- [Waveform implementation — PJRC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PaulStoffregen/Audio/3039be2773e86daf1f381a1e8bdc1e6a55ed11f1/synth_waveform.cpp)
- [Teensy Audio Library — PJRC](https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_libs_Audio.html)

lessons.title: ADSR stages and linear segments
lessons.body:
A note isn't just a pitch and a timbre; it has a shape in time. A piano note strikes and decays, an organ note starts and stops abruptly, a pad swells. The **envelope** generates that shape as a control signal, usually driving the amplifier (loudness) and often the filter cutoff (brightness).

The same maths solves a second problem: when a knob or MIDI controller changes a parameter in steps, the audio must not step with it. That's **parameter smoothing**.

## ADSR

The classic envelope has four controls, triggered by the key's **gate** (on while held):

- **Envelope attack:** time to rise from the current level to the peak after the key goes down.
- **Decay stage:** time to fall from the peak to the sustain level.
- **Sustain level:** a *level* (not a time), held while the key stays down.
- **Envelope release:** time to fall to zero after the key is released.

```diagram
level
 1.0 |   /\
     |  /  \___________  <- sustain
     | /               \
 0.0 |/                 \____
     +--A--D-----S------R---> time
     gate on      gate off
```

### Linear segments

The simplest implementation moves the level by a fixed step per sample. For an attack from 0 to 1 the step is the total rise divided by the number of samples the attack lasts:

```formula
Δy = 1 / (T_a f_s)
Δy = 1 / (0.01 s × 48000 Hz) = 1 / 480
where
Δy: delta y, how much the level rises each sample
T_a: the attack time, in seconds (s); here 10 ms = 0.01 s
f_s: the sample rate, in hertz (Hz): samples per second, here 48,000
s: seconds
Hz: hertz, per second
In words: spread the rise from 0 to 1 evenly over the attack's samples; a 10 ms attack at 48 kHz lasts 480 samples, so each adds 1/480.
```

Decay and release work the same way, using the distance they have to travel. It's easy to reason about, and each segment ends at a precise time.

Linear segments have a drawback for amplitude: hearing is roughly logarithmic, so a linear fade in *amplitude* sounds like it hangs on, then vanishes abruptly at the end. Linear attacks often sound fine; linear releases and decays often sound unnatural.

## Key takeaways

- Sustain is a level; attack, decay and release controls describe transitions.
- Linear ramps spread a chosen distance across a fixed number of samples.

## Further reading

- [Envelope generators — Nigel Redmon](https://www.earlevel.com/main/2013/06/01/envelope-generators/)
- [Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog](https://cdn.inmusicbrands.com/Moog/Model%20D/Minimoog_Model_D_Manual.pdf)
